utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Proceedings were delayed again today due to technical difficulties. I would like to go back to an issue Mr. Robinson raised yesterday with respect to the Prosecution's contact with Defence witnesses. At the end of your submission, Mr. Robinson, you stated, I quote, it's transcript page 30105, lines from 11 to 14, it reads: "However, I wanted to put it on the record and ask Mr. Tieger to make sure that all members of the Prosecution not only in his team but any other teams that might have any potential need to contact these witnesses to comply with the Trial Chamber's order." So I was wondering what you meant by "any other teams"? Did you mean to say that, for example, Mladic team should also comply with our Chamber's order? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. President, because the Prosecution is one so they have to comply with disclosure obligations and other things regardless of whether they come into contact in the context of one case or another. In particular, this matter arose in relation to the Tolimir case because we were advised that the two witnesses who the Prosecution wanted to contact first and one of whom who they had inadvertently already contacted were to be contacted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is simply unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe we can move to courtroom 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we have to just adjourn. We have to rise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is also unacceptable that ... [In English] It appears to be that what Mr. Robinson said is unacceptable, but I assume that Excellency Kwon said about technical ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise until we are further informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, again. I have to find out which computer is mine. Does it mean that we lost all of the previous transcript for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to check until where it has been recorded. So shall we start again? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think where I left off was that we consider the Prosecution to be one for purposes of contacting our witnesses -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: My microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's my fault. I inadvertently the priority switch. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, so Mr. President, it's our position that since the Prosecution is one, that the Prosecution has to comply with your order regardless of whether it's a member of the Karadzic team or the member of another team. And I had indicated to you that the issue first arose last week when I was advised by one of the members of the Prosecution team that people from the Tolimir team wanted to interview two witnesses who are on our list. And so they contacted us pursuant to your order and we contacted the witnesses and now we've advised the Prosecution that they're free to make contact with the witness. So the system worked well except for the inadvertent contact by the Prosecution, and we believe that that system should continue to be in place for any contacts by members of any Prosecution team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just two questions, preliminary questions. First one is for you, Mr. Robinson. When you refer to inadvertent contact by the Prosecution team, did you mean the contact of the Tolimir team with Defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, it was an investigator who's working on this case but also working on Tolimir case, and I was advised by the Prosecution that he had made contact with the witness without fully understanding the extent of the Trial Chamber's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it concerned the investigation -- an investigator in the Karadzic OTP team?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, not entirely, Mr. -- technically, yes, that's true, but it was the same investigator who's been working for the Tolimir team and this was a contact made for the -- at the behest of the Tolimir team. And in fact, this was a matter in which the OTP acted very efficiently on both fronts, it seems to me, that is, notifying members of the team and, indeed, members of other teams about this Court's order, but also this particular investigator in the Tolimir team moving quickly on the contact. So when there's -- as Mr. Robinson is well aware, there's nothing purposefully violative of the Court's order. Quite the contrary. Everyone -- the Karadzic team acted as quickly as possible to alert people. So this was just a matter where the Tolimir team asked this particular investigator to undertake contact before the investigator had been made aware of the terms of the Court's order. So I -- and I think Mr. Robinson fully appreciates that. There's no suggestion to the contrary, as far as I'm aware. If I may also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tieger, probably this question is not meant for you, but what sounds odd to me is this: Why does the Tolimir team need to interview witnesses at all, given the stage of its case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I -- I can't -- I'm not in a position to answer on behalf of the parties who -- of Mr. McCloskey in this case who is the head of the Tolimir team or anyone else who is involved in this particular effort. But I can think of various reasons why that would be the case. If these particular witnesses are thought to have information or to be about to bring information to the attention of this Trial Chamber which somehow implicates some evidence or significant evidence in the Tolimir case, that might well be something that the Tolimir team would want to know early rather than late. The Court is well aware of the fact that, for example, 115 motions are brought well after judgement, so sometimes there can be reasons to move with alacrity when there's any indication that there is information that may be in existence that hasn't previously been brought to the attention of the parties or the Trial Chamber. In any event, that's one of the possibilities. I don't want to speak for them, but let me simply say if there's any suggestion that they were acting at the behest of the Karadzic team, that is not at all the case. So they weren't -- so this was an independent interest on their part. If I could -- as long as I'm up on my feet, if I could add one thing, Mr. President, and that is that we essentially share the -- what I think is the Trial Chamber's puzzlement about the theoretical basis for Mr. Robinson's position. There are some matters in which the OTP is one, but Trial Chambers have reserved the right to establish procedural standards and rules for how those -- their cases will be run; and therefore, it's very obvious that the OTP is subject to varying rules and standards and guide-lines and practices from case to case. And we do not consider that the -- this Trial Chamber intended to bind other Trial Chambers in their determination of how the OTP in those cases should make contact with witnesses. The ultimate absurdity of that argument, it seems to me, is the fact that some of the witnesses on the Defence witness list are also witnesses, as I understand it, for the Prosecution in the Mladic case. So the attempt to blur those distinctions and act as if there aren't separate Trial Chambers in existence and separate trials running I think is clearly inappropriate, as reflected in that example. Having said that, we don't want there to be unnecessary problems and problems where they don't need to exist. And that's why we are willing to contact other teams and to the extent possible see if we can ensure that contact is -- that we co-ordinate this and we don't make contact before notifying Mr. Robinson. So we're happy to be as accommodating as possible and eliminate problems where they don't need to arise, but we reject the notion that we are under any obligation to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope this is just a storm in a teacup, but when we order the Prosecution to give notice to the Defence we never meant to include the other OTP teams. But the crux of the reasoning why the Chamber ordered the Prosecution to give notice to the Defence when they would like to meet with the witnesses whose contact detail they have already is out of courtesy and some practical reasons. So if the Prosecution is minded to co-operate on a voluntary basis, we would encourage very much that such practice continue in the future as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then unless there's anything to be raised, then we'll bring in the next witness. In the meantime, I think it has been circulated, but to make sure, we'll sit for the first session till quarter past 11.00 and we'll have a 15 minutes' break, after which we'll have a second session which will last until 12.50. And then we'll have a 40 minutes' lunch break and we'll sit from 1.30 to 3.00, at which time the Chamber has to rise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, I'd just like to suggest that this witness be provided with a caution under Rule 90(E). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just out of an abundance of caution, I state this because I'm not sure whether what you stated is recorded or not. Mr. Karadzic, what you said was correct. What I said "unacceptable" was the technical difficulties but not what Mr. Robinson submitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, before you start giving evidence I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution, the accused, or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the answer. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood that fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D6087 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear on the screen, Mr. Tomic, I'd like to ask you whether you provided the Defence team with a statement?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement on the screen before you now?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind myself and I have to ask you to make pauses between what we're saying for the benefit of the interpreters. Does this statement accurately reflect what you knew and what you stated?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom, would your answers be more or less the same?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: My answers would be identical to the answers that I gave for the purpose of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, may I tender this statement into evidence as well as the 92 ter package to be admitted through Witness Mr. Bozo Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson, 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We would ask for permission to add the map that the witness marked, which is 1D0034, to our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, and there's no objection to the admission of any of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we upload the second one, the 1D20540, so that we can take a brief look. What's the date of this document, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, English translation says it's 3rd of May, so it may have to be corrected. Shall we upload it, 1D20540. Yes. Your statement, Mr. Karadzic, that the date is 9th of May seems to be sufficient. We'll continue on that basis. So we'll admit the statement as well as four -- five associated exhibits. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 1D6087, the statement, will be Exhibit D2418. 65 ter number 1D134 will be Exhibit D2419. 65 ter number 1D20540 will be Exhibit D2420. 65 ter number 1D20544 will be Exhibit D2421. 65 ter number 1D20301 will be Exhibit D2422. And 65 ter number 1D20548 will be Exhibit D2423.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to read a brief summary of Mr. Tomic's statement in English. [In English] Bozo Tomic was a member of the command of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. He did his military service in the JNA in 1981 and 1982 in Pula and then on the island of Molat. He left the JNA with the rank of private first class. After the events in March 1992, when the Serbian wedding guest was killed in Bascarsija and barricades were set up in the city, he found out that many Muslims had been summoned for some military exercises. Sometime later he was told that there were training camps for Muslim paramilitary units on Mount Igman. He lived on Ozrenska Street in a Serb majority area. In early April 1992, he and several of his neighbours agreed on the need to organise themselves to protect their families and property. Roughly at the same time, members of the Serbian Territorial Defence told him and them to organise guards on the streets, to be particularly vigilant at night, and they received signs of recognition to distinguish people outside the neighbourhood and their basic task, as before, was to protect their houses and families. He was elected squad commander. From the very beginning of the conflict, Muslims opened fire on them from the sector of Sanac and Pero Kosoric Square from multi-storey buildings. All residential buildings in Pero Kosoric Square and individual houses above and under Tranzit Street, as well as other civilian buildings, were used for military purposes by establishing in them enemy firing positions. Muslim sniper fire had disastrous consequences on the Serbian side, both soldiers and civilians alike, and not even children were spared. Because of this, his unit built protection out of tarpaulin, nylon, cardboard, hard material, among others, to conceal movement and hinder reconnaissance and enemy fire. The Muslim forces ranging against them continuously planned and executed offensive combat operations against his unit's line of defence. They never received any order or instructions referring to the expulsion of non-Serbs from their houses and apartments. Around mid-May 1992, as the war grew in intensity, several Muslim families from Ozrenska Street moved completely unhindered and without duress to the part of the town under Muslim control. They had no -- the Serbs in this company had no intention of causing civilian casualties, of exercising psychological influence on civilians under Muslim control, neither did his superior commands. They never received any oral or written order from higher commands or civilian authorities to carry out attacks against civilians under control of the Muslim authorities. Likewise, he never issued any such orders. They only carried out defensive actions and never opened fire into the depth of the enemy territory, firing only on the line of disengagement and exclusively on military targets which directly threatened them. Because of the difficulty of the front and the small number of men in Ozrenska Street, they contacted the brigade command asking for reinforcements for the line and the engagement of a work detail to fortify the line. The work detail was comprised of Muslims who came from Kula penal and correctional facility and were treated properly. There were no professional soldiers in his unit. It was a real people's army comprised of the people from Ozrenska Street and the neighbourhood. By the end of the war, about 220 people were killed and several hundreds wounded in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Battalion. [Interpretation] For the time being, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tomic, as you have noted that your evidence in chief was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be asked by the Prosecution in its cross-examination. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tomic. I'd like to start by asking you a couple of questions --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking you a couple of questions about the background to the conflict. At paragraph 4 of your statement you said: "With the war in Croatia, a different atmosphere began to be felt in Sarajevo. My experience was that it was loaded with a negative charge, sincere socialising stopped and divisions along ethnic lines were felt. Speeches of Muslim and Croatian politicians in the Assembly created an atmosphere of mistrust and fear." What particular speeches of Muslim and Croat politicians in the Assembly created, in your view, an atmosphere of mistrust and fear?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, right this minute I can't remember all the politicians and their speeches, but the president of the Party of Democratic Action, Mr. Izetbegovic, and the president of Herceg-Bosna or the Croatian Democratic Union, Mate Boban, were very unpleasant. I'm speaking from the point of view of the Serbian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you could guess that there was this so-called unprincipled coalition between the Muslim and Croatian people. All -- and they saw Serbs - although it was illogical - as their common enemy. In any case, fear and anxiety were rising and particularly in view of their memories from the Second World War Serbs felt that they had to unite and organise themselves because they could not feel safe in that country. The practice of out-voting one people in the Assembly was another reason for this rising anxiety and fear. I had personal experience as well at my work-place.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats united on one side and --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Tomic, but I think we're straying away from the question which was about speeches of politicians in the Assembly. And I understand from your answer that you can't recall any specific statements, but they were very unpleasant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Izetbegovic was always prepared to sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. We Serbs are not naive and especially with our experience from previous wars, we knew what that meant. We didn't need anyone to explain to us what it meant when he said that we will sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina of his vision, Serbs had nothing good to expect.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And what about statements of Serb politicians in the Assembly, do you recall any speeches of Serb politicians in the Assembly that added to this atmosphere of mistrust and fear in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, I could say that it was taken out of the context of the speech of the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic, is something that I understood as a warning especially after the Lisbon Agreement or the Cutileiro Plan as it was known. I, myself, my neighbours, and my friends thought that it was a good basis for an agreement that could spare us from a horrible war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if I remember correctly, Mr. Izetbegovic even put his initials on that document; however, upon returning to Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- he reneged on it and I believe it was after he was influenced by some other factors, especially foreigns.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, I think we're moving away from the topic, but you did allude to a speech of Mr. Karadzic and I assume you're talking about his speech from October of 1991 where he stated that Bosnia was taking the same highway of hell and suffering that Croatia and Slovenia went through and warned of the possible extinction of the Muslim people if it came to war. Is that the speech you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that speech. But I'm saying in Slovenia there were far fewer Serbs as a minority than in the Serbian population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I understood him as saying that Serbs, of course, would suffer a lot in case of war, but Muslims would suffer the most. If I had heard something like that from Mr. Izetbegovic, I would - although a Serb - be grateful for such a statement and I would understand it as meaning that all of us should make certain compromises to avoid war. However, I also have to say, as I did in my statement, I played football every day at the Grbavica stadium and some friends with whom I used to play without even knowing their ethnicity --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- were missing. You can only imagine how I felt when I learned --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again I interrupted you because we are moving away from the question. If you could try to focus as specifically as possible on the precise question. Now, notwithstanding your apparent claim that you would be grateful for a statement from Mr. Izetbegovic warning the Serb people of their possible extinction, Mr. Karadzic's warning to the Muslim people of their possible extinction when it came to war added to the atmosphere of mistrust and fear in Sarajevo, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Muslims probably understood it that way; I did not. And, you see, I can't answer your questions with a yes or no. I need to explain certain things. This is not a mathematical problem where I only have to explain a formula. I have to say one thing. Alija Izetbegovic and the Muslim leadership had already called upon their young people not to join the Yugoslav People's Army. I and most Serbs saw Yugoslavia as our homeland and that was therefore something unusual, something that was happening for the first time that Muslims were not joining that army, while at the same time making paramilitary units, organising training camps, and I later found out that they had started preparing as early as 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- we were not doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, I understand you feel the need to explain, but that really isn't responsive to the question, which you did answer in the first line of your answer. Thank you. Okay. I'd like to move on now to April 1992, and you stated that you lived in Ozrenska Street and in the immediate vicinity of the MUP school. So your home and the MUP school, they were in Vraca, in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the clashes of the MUP school that you referred to in paragraph 6, those clashes were in connection with the Bosnian MUP special forces taking over the school in Vraca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know any details, but I know that members of the special unit whose purpose was to intervene in case of emergencies in the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there too Muslims and Croats left and went elsewhere, whereas only Serbs remained. That night of the 4th April, from the direction of Sanac and from the direction of Pero Kosoric Square and the Tranzit company, fire was opened onto our area. One Serb, a member of that special unit, was killed and two were wounded. I myself was not involved. It was an operation of those so-called special forces, and I did not participate; but I learned that one of them got killed. And it was an internal conflict within a unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina and because of various disagreements and --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic. I understand from your answer that, indeed, the MUP special forces were there and there was an operation involving them at the time. I think that's sufficient to answer my question so I'll move on to the next question. You said at paragraph 7 of your statement: "We found out that members of the Serbian TO were in the Pajaco restaurant at the beginning of Ozrenska Street." Now, Pajaco, as I understand it, that's also in the immediate vicinity of your house and the MUP school in Vraca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: It's closer to the MUP school, whereas my house is perhaps 300 metres from that restaurant called Pajaco.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And Pajaco, was that the headquarters of the Novo Sarajevo Serbian TO?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the headquarters of Novo Sarajevo TO, but I know that when I went there to inquire with my neighbours whether we needed to organise ourselves, we were told that they were members of the TO and we were issued with weapons. Of course, we were under a lot of pressure and we were very anxious, expecting something to happen, so we wanted to get armed to be able to protect our families and our neighbourhoods, all of us who lived in Ozrenska Street. Whether that was the headquarters of Novo Sarajevo TO, I really don't know. I know that some people were there, and when we were issued with weapons, my comrades selected me to be some sort of squad commander and I was given an automatic rifle. Every day at dusk we would go there to take certain distinction marks, as is the custom in every army, to be able to tell that we were from that area, both Muslims and Serbs, only for the purpose of protecting the local population, all of us who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could -- just a comment on the transcript. The witness said: In order to be able to protect our families, all of us who lived there regardless of faith and ethnicity. And that was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just on that point, Mr. Tomic, you stated that this was the -- in your statement that this was the Serbian TO. Were there Muslims and Croats going to Pajaco restaurant, where - as you state - the Serbian TO was located?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know if any Muslims went there. I went with a group of my neighbours and they didn't even have enough weapons for all of us. They gave us some to be able to have them at guard duty at night and of course that line was not properly organised according to --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- all military regulations. So I went there with people from my closest circle. I don't know if there were any Muslims involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Tomic. Ms. Gustafson is asking questions following your statement. Do you have your statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not this minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to have one in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be a good idea if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, that will be done. Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you've stated several times now in your answers that it was at Pajaco that you received -- you and your neighbours received weapons. Who at Pajaco was distributing weapons to you and your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I know that Budo Obradovic, Momir Garic were there. I didn't even know all those people because it's impossible to know them all. And we were told that our task was - and I said before it was also our desire - to protect our families. We were expecting that something could happen any time. We just wanted to prevent war. I don't know the names of all those people. And I'm saying again there were not enough weapons for all of my neighbours, so sometimes somebody would have to borrow a weapon and of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- there were not enough automatic weapons, not even semi-automatic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, we're straying away from the topic. I wasn't asking you about the quantity of weapons. Now, you mentioned Budo Obradovic and Momir Garic. Were Budo Obradovic and Momir Garic distributing weapons and giving you tasks from Pajaco?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: My neighbours and I had heard that there was something at Pajaco. I don't know if it was the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- headquarters Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You're now repeating your earlier answer. My answer [sic] was very specific. It was: "Were Budo Obradovic and Momir Garic distributing weapons and giving you tasks from Pajaco?" If you could answer that with a "yes" or a "no," please.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I've already said, let's not exaggerate. I don't know if Budo or Momo gave me the weapons, but they were there and we were given a specific task. We wanted to and they advised us to protect our families, to prevent incursions from outsiders, strangers, that's what it was about. There was no real military organisation yet. We were just self-organising. I cannot tell you specifically whether Budo or Momo or Marko or whoever gave me the weapon. All I know that there was this -- I don't know if it was the headquarters of Novo Sarajevo TO or it was only for the local commune, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you said you didn't know if it was Budo or Momo who gave you the weapons, you're referring to Budo Obradovic and Momir Garic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say, the witness said in line 3: Or somebody else, and that was not recorded. All that was left was whether it was Momo or Budo -- or somebody third is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's the case -- do you confirm that, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm saying I can't even remember whether one of the two or both were there on that particular day. Perhaps they had been there, but it's pointless for me to claim now, 20 years later, that either of them specifically gave me the weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it's confirmed by Ms. Gustafson but I'd like to confirm with you once again, Momir Garic's nickname was Momo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I know him, as Momo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now again you've referred both in your statement and several times in your answers so far to Momir Garic and Budo Obradovic at Pajaco. I understand from that that they were either the commanders or the leaders of your TO unit in Novo Sarajevo; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't speculate. I don't know what their assignments were. I just told you the truth about how we went there and received weapons. There was no military organisation yet. Only later did the 1st Omladinska Brigade -- sorry, 1st Romanija Brigade came and towards the end of May the 1st Mechanised Sarajevo Brigade was established and we joined it - me and my comrades - and remained till the end part of that 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you said that when you went to Pajaco you were given a specific task, and that was at lines 3 and 4 of page 20; and also in your statement you said you were told at Pajaco to organise guards in the street, et cetera. Who at Pajaco gave you these tasks?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: That was said once. We didn't need telling twice --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- we organised ourselves to go every day and take --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- whether it was -- whether you were told once or multiple times, that's not the question. Who told you? Who gave you these tasks?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, we received tasks, instructions, but we had asked ourselves to be given them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, and who gave you the tasks?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps one of those two, but I'm telling you we asked ourselves for our own safety and the safety of our families and all the inhabitants of that street in order to feel safe, because at night it happened in some parts of the city that outsiders, perhaps criminals or robbers, would --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- barge in and we had to protect ourselves from looting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? The interpretation the witness received was in a continuous form of the verb "to give," "who gave you instructions" instead of the one-time form [In English] "Who used to give us -- to give you," "who used to give you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That may be the reason -- but, Mr. Tomic, could you concentrate on answering the question. Let's continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have -- sorry, Exhibit D2419 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, the map that you're about to see on the screen is the map that you marked in connection with your statement where you indicated with a red line the Serbian positions in Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in on the red line which is roughly in the middle of the page and a little bit down. If we could zoom in a little more. And maybe one more time so the line is clear. And if we could move the map to the right and up -- sorry, the other way, and down so we can see. Yeah, great.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, can you see the line, the red line, that you drew?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: That's -- if that's the line going through the football stadium and via Tranzit and this elevation Sanac and along Ozrenska Street, yes, I drew that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to mark where you, in particular, were positioned in April 1992 on Ozrenska Street on this map?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: That's precisely the part going above Tranzit, above that road and the football stadium, going towards this hill, Sanac, and up to Ozrenska Street and further. Until May 1994, I was a member of the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade. A friend of mine and I were in command of a platoon of about 60 men. We had our area of responsibility within the 3rd Company. That's precisely the line I marked on the map that went, as I said, from Tranzit and covered Tranzit, while a neighbouring platoon was at the beginning of the stadium, that is to say, closer to the police school and Grbavica. Just to make one thing clear, the street that goes from Grbavica towards Miljacka was Djuraskovica Street. There was company Strojorad and it goes along the left bank of the Miljacka river and that was the area of responsibility of the 2nd Battalion whose commander I was from 1994 until the end of the war. So that's the line I also marked that goes down towards Lukavica. That's one of the longest streets in the city, Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I understand from your answer - and correct me if I'm wrong - that the positions you held in April, basically you continued to hold the same positions when you were a member of a platoon of the SRK and that those -- that position covered the entire length of the line that you've drawn on this map in red. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, our battalion had within the 3rd Company of the 1st Romanija Brigade its area of responsibility. It was a stretch about several hundred kilometres, and until 1994 I spent all my time there, leaving Sarajevo a few times going towards Trnovo and the Niksic plateau. So there were trips like that in order to reinforce our unit, but most of the time I spent there, on this stretch of several hundred metres. And the task of our platoon was to hold that defence line. And during the war, that line did not move. There were no offensive actions in my unit, we were not advancing, and as time went by --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- we only fortified it --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really have to ask you to limit your answers to the specific questions that I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you need more time to finish your cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll take a break now for 15 minutes and resume at 32 past 11.00. But I have to note that I forgot to mention that we were sitting for the first session pursuant to 15 bis due to Judge Lattanzi's official function. She will join us from the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, this may be the first time for four Judges to be fit into Courtroom 2. Ms. Gustafson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, I'd like you now to watch a video and this is P5062. It has no sound so I'd just like you to watch what appears on your screen and we will stop it at 28 seconds and then I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, in this video you've seen Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic entering a military position and now we can see the view from that position. This is a shot from a position at Ozrenska Street looking out over Grbavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd said from some other position a bit to the right of Ozrenska. According to the buildings I can see here, I assume it's some sort of observation post, that it is from that location that the positions were observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you say "to the right," what do you mean? Do you mean to the east or to the west?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a little to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you believe this is east of Ozrenska Street in Vraca?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I would say that it's in Vraca, given the angle of observation and the buildings you can see because there are no such elevations in Ozrenska. So I would say that it is somewhere to the right. That is how I would interpret this photograph, this image.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But Ozrenska Street is -- runs along a hill and overlooks Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: But I'm just speaking about the angle from which this image was recorded. I would say that it's an elevation in relation to Ozrenska Street, so to the right or to the east of Ozrenska Street in the direction of Vraca, perhaps in the direction of Trebevic, let's say, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could continue playing this video and that was, for the record, 28 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And we've stopped at 52 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, can you confirm that this is another view of Grbavica, and those three high-rises with the white on the edges, that's Soping?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the distance towards the horizon you can see the Hum hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, we're finished with that video. Mr. Tomic, you have emphasised, both in your statement and in your evidence earlier today, that in April, when you were a member of the Novo Sarajevo TO, that your tasks were solely about protecting your homes and neighbourhoods and that there was no offensive action. It is the case, is it not, that in April there was a TO offensive towards the north of the positions that you have marked on your map as the line of defence and into -- in particular an offensive in the Grbavica area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: In the area of the unit that I was a member of at the time when it entered the 1st May unit there were no defensive or offensive actions, but in second part, yes, in Grbavica at the time because there were a lot of Serbs living there. People organised themselves down there to protect themselves, their families, and their property, and in order to be safe in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm talking about a Novo Sarajevo Serb TO offensive on the 21st of April, 1992, in Grbavica. Was there or was there not such an offensive?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I didn't participate in any such offensive. I was at the lines that I have marked, at the positions I marked. Our task was to hold the positions there, to protect the area where we lived, my neighbours, my friends, from the street. So I did not participate in that offensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you recall that offensive, the 21st of April offensive, in Grbavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the date, but I know it was towards the end of April. I wouldn't say that it's the 21st, but if you say so, it's quite possible. However, I did not take part in that offensive. I wouldn't say that it was an offensive operation. The people organised themselves and did the same things that we did in Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the TO from Vraca went down to Grbavica and attempted to take territory in Grbavica. That's an offensive; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No, there were a lot of Serbs in Grbavica and even the municipality of Novo Sarajevo itself before the war was inhabited by a majority of Serbs. The municipality covered a large area, and the majority of the inhabitants in Grbavica were Serbs. They organised themselves as did we. They were there. There were no forces from the outside, no members of the Territorial Defence from the outside. They all had their responsibility in given sectors, in certain areas of the Vraca local commune where they lived because the municipality covered an entire area and Ozrenska Street was part of Vraca local commune, part of the area was part of the Hrasno local commune, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not able to follow your answer. Do you agree or disagree that members of the TO from Vraca went down to Grbavica to attempt to take territory?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: As I said, I don't agree because I know that in Grbavica there were a lot of Serbs who lived in the area and they also organised themselves as did we in Ozrenska Street and in other parts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to listen to an intercept which is Exhibit D1202. And, Mr. Tomic, this is an intercepted telephone conversation from the 21st of April, 1992, if you could listen to it and then I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "MG: Good afternoon. "NN: Good afternoon. "MG: May I speak to Danilo? "NN: Danilo? "MG: Yes. "NN: Danilo who? "MG: Veselinovic. "NN: Well, you got the wrong number, my son. Where are you calling from? "MG: And is Prstojevic there? "NN: Who are you and where are you calling from? "MG: I'm calling from Novo Sarajevo. "NN: And you are? "MG: Momo. "NN: Momo who? "MG: Garic. "NN: I beg your pardon? "MG: Garic. "NN: Tell me, Eric. "Come on Garic, come on -- "MG: Wait, wait, wait a second. Garic. This is Garic. "NN: Oh, Garic. Go ahead. "MG: Is Veselinovic there? "NN: No, Veselinovic is not here, but here is -- "MG: Well, can you just -- how can you help us, please? "NN: Tell me, speak up. "MG: The army refuses, those tanks, we are encircled. Do you have any armour, any manpower? Please, I'm begging you. "NN: Garic, Prstojevic is here. "MG: Let me talk to him. "UMP: They dumped the armour, three men in 'Palma' -- "NP: Hello. "MG: Prstojevic? "NP: Yes. "MG: This is Garic. "NP: Good morning. "MG: What's up? Listen. "NP: Nothing special. "MG: How can you help us as soon as possible? "NP: Help who? "MG: Us. "NP: Who? Where is that? "MG: Novo Sarajevo. "NP: Yes, but where? What is your location? "MG: Just a second. In Vraca. We need some men in Vraca urgently, please. "NP: But wait a second, where are you in Vraca exactly? Are you down near the MUP or up there? "MG: We are -- somebody will wait for these men at the pass. "NP: Are you up at the pass and further up on the right side? "MG: I will wait for the men at the pass. "NP: Wait a second, Garic. Are you at the pass and further up on the right side, towards Vraca? "MG: We went down to the town, all the way to the Miljacka, however, they are too strong there. They are encircling us and the army refuses to move. "NP: Wait a second. Are you fighting there? "MG: We are fighting fiercely. We have many casualties. "NP: Tonight, is that right? "MG: Well, no, we started this morning here ... forget about it, now we are encircled, as it seems. "NP: Mm-hmm. "MG: How can you help us? I also called Velibor in Nedzarici and he will try to do something, but that is not enough. That is not enough. "NP: All right. What are the Special Forces doing? "MG: They refuse to leave the barracks. The Special Forces refuse to leave the barracks area. That's it. The reserve police force also promised to do everything they can but they went back. "NP: Aha. "MG: That's it. What are we going to do? "NP: You know, it's day-time and it's the south, and it is difficult to fight during the day in the south. "MG: Yes. "NP: And if they encircle you ... okay, we cannot allow that. First of all, we must not allow the encirclement and second -- "MG: Yes, yes. "NP: -- one can strike very well during day. "MG: Yes. "NP: So you have to organise yourself and get help from people from the nearest surroundings. "MG: There is nobody closer than you. "NP: You have Vraca, Petrovici, and that area. "MG: There is nobody here. They've all gone down. "NP: They've all gone down? "MG: Yes. "NP: Well, if everybody's gone down, those must be very strong forces. "MG: Well, them. We are stretched thin on other sides, Zlatiste up there. "NP: Yes. "MG: So that is the problem. That is the problem. "NP: Withdraw. I don't know now, at this hour, things here are going -- "MG: What? "NP: I don't know if we can give you any specific help right now. "MG: Yes. "NP: At this moment. "MG: All right. All right. "NP: Where are you fighting exactly? Where exactly are you? "MG: Vrbanja, Grbavica, Ivan Krndelj, and all the way to Elektroprivreda. "NP: And you went down, is that right? "MG: Yes, yes. "NP: Aha. "MG: Yes. "NP: Well, if nothing else, withdraw a little bit. Be resilient, I mean. "MG: Yes. "NP: Withdraw and mobilise all those people. "MG: Yes, yes, everybody has been mobilised. "NP: Don't forget that it is difficult to send men to fight in an unknown area. "MG: Yes, yes, all right. All right. "NP: All right then. "MG: All right. Bye."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, the -- here you heard Momo Garic calling from Novo Sarajevo and specifically from Vraca. He's trying to reach Prstojevic. He explains that he is encircled. He describes his position. He said: "We went down to the town all the way to the Miljacka river." He says: "We are fighting fiercely, we have many casualties." He's describing, is he not, a Novo Sarajevo TO operation where TO members from Vraca have gone down to fight in an offensive operation in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps someone from the Territorial Defence participated in it. But in Grbavica there was a sufficient number of locals, Serbs above all, who organised themselves, and I traced a red line. You can see how large the area of Vraca is. The unit I was in wasn't directly above Grbavica. If we left our positions, the area would have remained empty. That line would have been penetrated and the entire area of Grbavica would have been encircled from all sides. So it wasn't possible for us to leave the defence line where we were located because the line was there, from the direction of Hrasno, behind Tranzit. The line was there and it was gradually fortified for the purpose of security, so we couldn't have participated in those operations. Our unit couldn't have done that. That would have resulted in leaving an area empty of -- that would have resulted in abandoning an area and the Muslims could have entered it. Someone may have assisted them, but I'm not familiar with that. I'm telling you that there were a sufficient number of people there who formed units later on and became part of the 1st Romanija Brigade in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in this intercept, Prstojevic -- by the way, did you know Nedjeljko Prstojevic, the commander of the Ilidza Crisis Staff, did you know him? I see you nodded, shook your head?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Prstojevic says: "So you have to organise yourself get help from people from the nearest surroundings." Garic says: "There is nobody closer than you." Prstojevic says: "You have Vraca, Petrovici, and that area." Garic responds: "There is nobody here, they've all gone down." Prstojevic asks: "They've all gone down?" And Garic says: "Yes." Here Mr. Garic is clearly describing a TO operation in which everyone from Vraca, Petrovici, and that area have gone down to Grbavica; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat what I said, that couldn't have been done. You couldn't leave the left or right flank without any men, just leave. Garic at that time certainly sustained significant casualties and he's a bit panicky, as you could see. He was asking for assistance. That's what I understood from the conversation that was intercepted, but it's not possible for everyone to go to just one part of the defence line. Then the right and left flank are abandoned and it can be penetrated --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- the area can be penetrated and what have you achieved then?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I understand your position is that notwithstanding these statements, that this was simply not possible. I'd like to move on now and talk about the time after your unit was absorbed into the SRK, which I understand from your statement is what happened. Now, you said earlier today that you were within the 3rd Company of the 2nd Battalion. The Chamber has heard some evidence that the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion was positioned on Ozrenska Street. Is it possible that you were a member of the -- that your platoon belonged to the 4th Company or can you otherwise explain -- reconcile that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to make something clear. The SRK was in the entire area of Sarajevo and it had a lot of brigades within it. The brigade that was formed in May 1992 was the 1st Romanija Brigade, and the company that I was a member of was the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade. The platoon I was a member of was the 2nd Platoon of that company. Subsequently, in spring, towards the end of May 1993, the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade was established and that 3rd Battalion was then the 2nd Infantry Battalion in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, and all those brigades in Sarajevo formed the SRK, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So my battalion or the company didn't become part of the SRK because you have platoons, company, battalions, brigade, and then the corps. That is the hierarchy that is established. That's how things work --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- in accordance with the establishment. So I was part of the 3rd Company --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your evidence now is that you were a member of the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade, which later became the 3rd Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. Can you explain where the 4th Company was positioned in relation to the 3rd Company? Because, as I said earlier, the Chamber's received evidence that the 4th Company was also on Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The 4th Company was there. In relation to the 3rd Company, it was to the left or to the west if you look at the map and it linked up with the 5th Company, whose area of responsibility was towards Mojmilo and Lukavica, and the 2nd Battalion was there - not in terms of establishment but a battalion from Dobrinja -- it was another battalion from Dobrinja, it wasn't the 2nd Battalion, but they were linked up. So the 4th Company was also in Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic. Again, if you could really try to focus on the specific question that I ask. Now I'd like to ask you about some of the locations where you indicate in your statement you were fired at from and that's at paragraphs 9 and 10 of your statement. And you included residential buildings and Pero Kosoric Square. That's a square in Hrasno; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the Loris building, that's also in Hrasno?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, it's in the direction of the Zeljeznicar football stadium. The red line that you see here shows that it's right next to the Milutin Djuraskovic Street, perhaps 50 metres from the Zeljeznicar football stadium in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the Plavi Neboder, or the blue skyscraper, where was that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Plavi Neboder, there were five of them, they were all on Pero Kosoric Square. These are all high positions in relation to our positions and sniper fire can cover the entire area of Ozrenska Street from there. These are skyscrapers that had about 20 floors.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So all of these locations were quite close to your positions on Ozrenska Street. Is that right? And if so, how close were they approximately?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time that I spent there in 1994, before I became a member of the battalion command. I spent all of that time in Sanac. It's within range of ordinary rifles and all large-calibre weapons, of course. The line of demarcation between us and the Muslim troops -- well, there was a distance of about 20 metres between us in certain areas. I'm talking about the area of this platoon exclusively, the platoon I was a member of from 1992 up until 1994 up until the end of May. But I know that in these other areas there was only the Miljacka river that represented the line of disengagement. So it was in the range of any kind of rifles or infantry weapons and even a house that I lived in, where my parents also lived, was in range of those infantry weapons and we spent the entire war time-period in that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the -- I understand then that the units positioned on this line and generally positioned on Ozrenska Street were exposed to a great deal of fire and were in a dangerous situation. Would you describe it as basically facing constant danger at those positions?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. The line that went along Ozrenska Street, it was interrupted at places wherever possible due to the configuration of the terrain. There is a huge number of houses there and each of the houses was a possible target, a possible place of incursion, or things like that. Along the entire length of Ozrenska Street, the distance between the two armies was 20 to 50 metres at the most. So you could even throw a stone -- we could throw stones at each other. Ozrenska Street had over 200 dead, unfortunately a lot of civilians among them died as a result of sniping or mortar fire that came from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said also in your statement that: "We never opened fire into the depth." When you say "we" here, are you talking just about your platoon or would you -- would you say that that's the case for all the units on Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I have to make a distinction here. Before 1994 I was a member of that unit and I can tell you for a fact that there was no fire opened in depth. After 1994 I can talk as a member of the battalion command and I can say that there was a strict order not to open fire in depth unless we were attacked; then we could use all means because we would be in full combat-readiness, we would all be on the line, and we would all be defending ourselves, so the situation was different then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So your position is that while you were a member of the platoon, there was no fire opened in depth. Do you mean that your -- nobody from your platoon opened fire into the depth?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You also identified some targets in the depth, that's at paragraph 19 of your statement and you talked -- you mentioned specifically schools on the right bank of the Miljacka and artillery pieces that were placed close to residential buildings. Did the units at Ozrenska Street face incoming fire from any of these positions in the depth that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: From Grbavica to -- or rather, from Soping, we set temporary observation posts, and since those were skyscrapers with 20 or so floors we could observe the other side. We could only observe, we couldn't do anything else, otherwise we would reveal our positions. And we could see all those facilities that I mentioned, and from all of them fire was opened on us. Later on we learned that they were involved in some dirty dealings. For example, they would affix a mortar to a little lorry, they would come to a building, fire a few shots, and then that lorry would be hidden behind a school or behind a building. Our observers saw that. It was impossible to find them later and it would have been in vain to open fire on those targets which were mobile, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you talked, just to follow-up on that, about the mortars on lorries. When you say it would be in vain to have opened fire on those targets, was that because by the time you're able to open fire on a mobile mortar like that it would have moved to another position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: The unit, or rather, the platoon at the beginning of the war and the battalion throughout the war did not have that kind of calibre, did not have that kind of tools with which it could return fire. Sometimes when there were skirmishes when they made attempts to break through our defence line, and sometimes they managed to do that, we asked for artillery support on the targets we observed and in places where members of the Muslim army gathered on their side. In other words, we did not have weapons that we could use against them; on our front line we only had infantry weapons, nothing else. Our biggest calibre was M84. We had some machine-guns M53 and 7.62-millimetre weapons. We didn't have cannons, we didn't have mortars with which we could jeopardise the targets we had observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. When you're saying that we only had -- our biggest calibre was an M84, we had no cannons or mortars, are you talking about your platoon or are you talking there about the battalion?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm primarily talking about the platoon before 1994. Later on in the battalion there were some weapons that could be used to provide support in certain positions during fierce combat and during attacks from their side. Then we indeed could ask for support and we received it. In companies there was a 60-millimetre mortar, smaller-calibre mortar. We didn't have bigger-calibre mortars, and in practical terms, it was impossible to use it because of the separation line where the distance was anything between 20 or 30 metres, not more. You couldn't ask for support from a bigger calibre because we would have threatened the lives of our soldiers because of the closeness between the two armies along the separation line that separated the two. Nobody is perfect. Nobody can aim so precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be clear, it is your possible that before 1994, nobody in the battalion had a bigger-calibre weapon than an M84; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I can't say this for a fact. I was in one of the units of the battalion. Perhaps in the battalion somebody had that; as far as I know, they didn't. But I don't know for a fact because I was not a member of any of the other units. It was impossible to move. I didn't know what the other units of the battalion were doing on the rest of the separation line. When you want to protect yourself from a mortar, there's no perfect way to do that. But when you moved along secure ways which were marked, where there were no roads, there were warnings to be aware of sniping, and people adhered to that --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- so in time there were less losses because people became more careful, more cautious.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, again, I'd like to interrupt you because we're moving away from the question that was asked. You did say in your statement at paragraph 23 that the UN military observers you dealt with never had any complaints about the firing of your battalion. And you said: "We in our unit did not even have any artillery weapons, and as for mortars, we only had 60-millimetre mortars." Now, I understand from that that you're talking about the 2nd Battalion and that your evidence is that in the entire 2nd Battalion there were no mortars of a calibre greater than 60 millimetres. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to now look at 65 ter 24044, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, the document you're about to see is a document from the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion on Ozrenska Street. So I understand from your earlier evidence this is not your company but it's the company further down the street. It's a list of weapons in the company dated the 22nd of October, 1993, at a time when you were also based on Ozrenska Street. And you can see that the list includes a PAM anti-aircraft machine-gun; three 60-millimetre mortars; an 82-millimetre mortar; a number of M84 and M53 weapons; three rocket-launchers; some M48s; and a Broving or Browning 12.7-millimetre heavy machine-gun. Now, this document shows not only did the 2nd Battalion have an 82-millimetre mortar, but the 4th Company, just down the road from you on Ozrenska Street, had one; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the date for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in 1993. I was a member of the platoon. I don't know what the company left my platoon had along -- not along Ozrenska Street but next to it. If I understand this properly, this was in 1993, and in 1994, at the beginning of June I became a member of the command of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson referred to the date. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: The year is 1993. I apologise, Your Excellency. In 1993 I was still not a member of the battalion command so I was not in a position to know whether those things existed in the 4th Company, whose member I was not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tomic, you've said that in 1994 no one in the entire battalion had a mortar greater than 60 millimetres. And we see from here already in 1993 the 4th Company had an 82-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you know that in 1994 the United Nations forces put a ban on the possession of weapons on the front line greater than 60 millimetres. All those weapons were moved in the depth of all the lines and members of UNPROFOR even attended some places from which it was potentially possible to open fire. So there was a ban on the possession of higher-calibre weapons in those areas. I don't know when that became effective. I know that it was in 1994 and the list of the weapons that existed in the 4th Company dates back to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, earlier you said that -- you said that the separation line where you were was 20 or 30 metres, not more. So these weapons on this list, in particular the mortars, those would have been used for firing at targets in the depth, beyond the confrontation line; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: 62-millimetre mortar is the only one that can provide support in fighting along the line which is only 30 metres deep. You can't use any greater calibre because shrapnel can fall on both sides. That's why the company that I belonged to before 1994, i.e., in that platoon, we did not have a calibre higher than 60 millimetre. And we're talking about 1993, you mentioned the 4th Company, I can see that this is the 4th Company. I didn't know that they had an 82-millimetre mortar that you mentioned and you showed me on this list of the weapons that the 4th Company allegedly had.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. Okay. So the 82-millimetre mortar on this list could only be used for firing at the depth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I can't speculate. I don't know whether they used it at all. Maybe they just had it at the ready for defence because there were many attempts at breakthroughs, there were lots of casualties in 1992 and 1993. I don't know whether they opened fire from it or not. I can't speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to follow-up on that, but just before we leave this document I'd like to confirm a couple more things with you. An M84 automatic weapon, that -- the effective range of that weapon is up to a thousand metres when it's mounted on a tripod; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And for an M53, its effective range is 1500 metres when it's on a tripod?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were such M53s, but they were not -- they were out of order, obsolete, which was made in 1953, it was not even safe to use. Unfortunately we did not have more M84s, that's why we had M53s, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And a 12.7-millimetre Browning heavy machine-gun, its range is about 1800 metres and 1500 metres for a point target; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't understand what your question is. Nobody will shoot at random if there is direct fighting. You use the weapons that you have on the defence line if you're attacked, but if the range of that weapon is what it is, why would you shoot arbitrarily and waste ammunition? We had a standing order to be careful about the use of ammunition which had to be economical. Why is the range important here? Why is it important whether this is 1200 or 1800 metres? I claim with full responsibility that the distance between the two armies along our separation line was 50 metres, 80 at the most at very few places, I'm talking about the battalion in which I spent the entire war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And early -- a few moments ago you said you couldn't speculate on whether the 82-millimetre mortar of the 4th Company was being used. You said maybe it was just on standby. So I'd like to look quickly at two more documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The first is 65 ter 24043.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And we can see this is a document from the 8th of June, 1993, from the 4th Company to the battalion command, reporting on the status of ammunition. And you can see it lists that there are seven 60-millimetre -- what's translated as grenades and six 82-millimetre grenades. That's a reference to mortar shells; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes. I suppose that's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could now turn to 65 ter 24045.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a document also from the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion about six months later on the 3rd of December, 1993, stating at the top "ammunition," and it includes one crate of 60-millimetre shells and two crates of 82-millimetre shells. And at the bottom it says: "We have none of the above-mentioned ammunition. I request that you deliver this ammunition to me." Now, these documents show that the 4th Company had ammunition for 82-millimetre mortars and was using it; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were using them, but I know that this document was drafted in 1993. I know that some platoon commanders or company commanders were afraid that they would not have enough and that's why they created reserves. This was in 1993. This is not my company but I'm aware of that situation. Sometimes you have to stock on certain things, for example, when you prepare food for winter you will want to stock up. This is a digression, but I know that some commanders did that to have what they needed in cases when it was needed. I don't know whether that was the case, but I suppose it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the last three documents that I've used, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question, Ms. Gustafson. I see the name here Dusan Zurovac, is he the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, even though the witness hasn't really confirmed them, we think that under the Chamber's ruling they're sufficiently related to his testimony that they can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I would add to that, Your Honour, it's direct impeachment of the witness's assertion that nobody in the battalion had an 82-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive them, three of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 24044 will be Exhibit P5983; 24043 will be Exhibit P5984; and 65 ter number 24045 will be Exhibit P5985.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at one further document, which is 65 ter 1D20334.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tomic, this is a report -- daily report from the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion, and it describes a commando raid in the area of the 4th Company position. It says: "Our commando group successfully took house after house, and so the line of disengagement in this locality was moved some hundred metres into the enemy depth. The enemy had artillery support, probably from Velesici, as we ascertained later when we analysed the trajectories of the shells that destroyed two civilian structures in the immediate vicinity of the command." And it says: "Our side didn't have any casualties ..." And it says: "Quite a lot of ammunition was expended" including ten mortar shells. Now, it's my understanding that these shells would not have been fired at the line of engagement because the commandos were there taking houses one by one. Are you able to tell us based on your knowledge of the situation what these ten mortar shells would have been fired at in this operation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Again, I can't speculate. That happened in 1993. This is not my unit. Maybe there was an attempt to break through from the Muslim side. Maybe they had to fortify the line or return the line. This is what I would say that would have happened in my unit if there was such attempts and if we had to return the line. I don't know whether they used shells and whether they fired them in the depth of the territory, as you say. All I claim is that it would be ineffective to fire shells in depth if your line was threatened. Nobody in their right mind would do that, especially not if they had some experience before that.
