That was in 1993, in June. What would that person have gained by firing shells in the depth of the territory when their line was threatened? But again, this was the 4th Company. I was a member of the platoon in the 3rd Company. That was my area of responsibility, so I believe that it is abundantly clear where I was at the time. That was very far from me, perhaps even a whole kilometre. I can't be sure. Maybe even 1500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5986, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, I'd like to move on to another topic which is the departure of non-Serbs from your neighbourhood that you speak about in your statement. And at paragraph 13 you said: "After the start of the conflict, near the MUP school I noticed that the Muslims from our street had withdrawn to their houses and that they were moving around much less. I went to the houses of my Muslim neighbours Suad Jazic, Senad Sabit, and Ibro Surkovic, and others. I wanted to know how they were feeling, if they had any problems, and if they were all right. All of them were scared and confused." Now, one of the factors contributing to their fear or the fear of non-Serbs in your area was the fact that non-Serbs from Serb-controlled parts of Sarajevo were being expelled; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any expulsion drives at that moment. I'm sure that they did not feel safe. They were afraid. I would have felt the same if I had been on the other side, because my sister with her son and her husband was on the other side and she felt the same until the end of May when she moved to the Serbian side and after that left Bosnia and Herzegovina all together. I believe that that would have been my motive for departure because I had lived with those people, with Senad Sabit, who were my friends. That's why I tried to help them as much as I could. I wanted them to feel safer if at all possible. I knew two other men, friends of mine, who were Croats. They left the area - I don't know how, during the night. Later on they contacted me after having left Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were both married. They are Croats. They were my very good friends and I wish them all the happiness like I do mine. It is absolutely understandable that people felt -- didn't feel safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There were at this time, were there not, expulsions of non-Serbs from Serb-held parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I'm talking about the street or the part of the street where I was and about specific people that I knew with whom I was very good friends. Whether it happened elsewhere, I suppose it did, on both sides. Everybody wanted to leave that area on the eve of any war. If you were in Syria now, you would want to flee. It's a normal human reaction, a normal desire to save yourself and your family. I cannot talk about any other parts of the city. I'm just talking about my street and the part of the street where I lived. These things did not happen there. I said in my statement I might have been on guard duty or elsewhere when my neighbours left the place. I'm sorry about that. I know, however - I was told later by friends of mine - that they were all safe and nothing bad happened to them, which is the most important thing in war, to survive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: They were escorted. [Interpretation] Again something is missing from the transcript: They were escorted. The witness said: They were escorted out so that nothing bad should happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, your answer suggested that these people were simply fleeing a war zone, but they were going from one side of the confrontation line to the city of Sarajevo, which was hardly escaping a war situation. These people, non-Serbs, were leaving your neighbourhood because of fear of what was happening around them, which was the expulsion of non-Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No. Emphatically no. Because I said my own sister was on the other side and in the same way she left voluntarily. Nobody made her. She was just thinking about her son and his safety and logically she wanted to save him from the war. My sister was not driven out either, nor were these other people. But I'm talking about the period when it was possible to cross from one side to another. It could have been until the end of May. Later on the city was completely blocked. Many who wanted to leave -- Serbs, Muslims, and Croats alike wanted to leave but it was no longer possible. Why? Because the Muslim leadership did not allow the Serbs to leave --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- I'm sure that many Muslims would have left Sarajevo even then if it had been possible, but it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Once again, we're moving away from the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to D92 and specifically page 66 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, this document is part of a speech that Mr. Prstojevic, who we -- was referenced in an earlier exhibit speaking with Momo Garic, was speaking in the Assembly, in the RS Assembly, in July 1992. And the B/C/S is not a very good quality so I will read out to you the relevant part. He says: "Namely, when the Serbs started the uprising in Sarajevo and when they seized control over certain territories, there was no government or at least it was not known where it was then. Moreover, we even did not know if Mr. Karadzic was alive during the first couple of days. When we learnt that he was alive and when he visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory, and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been majority." Now, this in a nutshell is what was happening in the early days of the war in Sarajevo and this is why the people -- the non-Serbs in your neighbourhood were afraid; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I see this document for the first time. I really never met Mr. Prstojevic myself, and of course this could be -- of course it is his speech, but what he meant I don't know. He was at Ilidza, as you say, so I don't know anything about this nor do I know that he spoke before the Assembly. I must say that I have never been a member of the SDS, but for me he was the leader of the movement because he was concerned about the survival of the Serb people. Why Mr. Prstojevic said this and spoke about some sort of expansion of the territory, I don't know. We had no offensive actions and we were just holding this defence line and the line did not move throughout the war. I am not aware of this speech, I'm not familiar with it, never heard it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But you did, in particular, at the end of the war or near the end of the war advocate for the Muslims who had left Grbavica to be prevented from returning there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know to what passage that relates, but I'm saying no. How can they return? The war was still on. You said "towards the end of the war," does it mean that the war was still ongoing or the war was over?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the war was basically over, and just after the Dayton Agreement was signed, which provided for Grbavica to be returned to the Federation side, you advocated for the Muslims to be prevented from returning there; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know if you have this information. A large number of Muslims spent the entire war at Grbavica; that is true, that is correct. At that point when the Dayton Accords have been signed, it's true what you say, Serbs had to leave Sarajevo. And how would we be in a position to prevent the Muslims from returning? I can't understand. How would we be in that position? How could we prevent them from coming back when the Dayton Accords have been signed, the demarcation lines were drawn, and it was clear which parts of Sarajevo belonged to whom. We had almost nothing; they had almost everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 22851, which I believe is an admitted exhibit and I'll just find the exhibit number now. If we could go to page 169 in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P1489, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if we could go to the B/C/S transcript rather than the original Cyrillic if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, this is an extract of General Mladic's military notebook, and it's -- records a meeting with SRK officers on the 22nd of December, 1995, and this is shortly after the Dayton Agreement was reached. And if we could go to the second page -- or sorry, the next page. And it says: "Second Lieutenant Bozidar Tomic." That's you; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Bozo, but that's what they called me, Bozidar. They also wrote Aleksandar, Aco, Sasa. I'm sorry, but I don't really see what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you see it now? Under your name it says: "People at Grbavica want to stay. "Guarantees that the Muslims and their police and authorities will not come ..." Now, this is a reference to you seeking guarantees that the Muslims would not return to Grbavica; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No. At that meeting I was present - that's a fact, that's true - and I sought guarantees that their police would not come to mistreat us because at that moment, all of us, the population of Grbavica and Vraca and I suppose other parts of the city where there were Serbs, Vogosca and Ilijas and such, wanted to remain in their homes, in their city. And we sought guarantees - maybe this was wrongly recorded, I don't know - not that Muslims would not come back to their homes; it was their indisputable right. I have to tell you, for seven years I was unable to get some of their families out of my own house, but we didn't want their authorities to come and make arrests among us. That's natural. I didn't mean that Muslims should not come, but that their police would not come to make searches and arrests. How could we feel safe at Grbavica even if we were allowed to stay in our homes? I suppose you know and you have that information that in my battalion Mr. Hrvatcevic, a captain who was deputy battalion commander when I was assistant commander, went to the international police force to work as an interpreter and he was arrested just a few days after he had started working. He was arrested, imprisoned, and mistreated, and spent four years in Zenica. How could we feel safe if their police and army were to arrive and make arrests and search houses --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- knowing that we were members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- again, I think we're straying from the question. I understand your position is that notwithstanding this reference to the Muslims and their and authorities, you were just referring to police and the authorities. I would like to move on now to talk about another topic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In general, your statement suggests that in your view the units that you belonged to and that were around you were familiar with the -- or complied with the laws of war. Were you familiar with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I had opportunity to read it once, but again, our soldiers were familiar with that, we were given this to read, and we always received strict orders. We in the battalion got orders from higher levels. It was strictly prohibited to open fire at civilian targets, against civilians, women and children in the city. Those are always the orders we received from our higher command, and the commander and his deputy issued such orders to company commanders and down -- further down to lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you would agree that the Geneva Conventions require, among other things, that civilians and prisoners of war be treated humanely and acts of violence and cruel treatment against such persons are prohibited; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And were you aware of any breaches of those conventions by any members of your units or other SRK units?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak about other units. I know that in my unit, although I can't claim with any certainty because the battalion had over 1.000 troops, it's too much for one establishment battalion, but the length of our line and the configuration of the line, required that number of troops. With time it varied --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- and was reduced because of our losses, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the configuration of your line. Are you aware of any breaches of the Geneva Conventions by any members of the units that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And are you aware of any inquiries or investigations for any of the units that you belonged to of any breaches of the Geneva Conventions or more generally of the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: There were no such cases in my unit. I'm saying again, I don't know but there were discipline procedures instituted against troops. The military police would intervene but that referred to breaches of public order, robberies, drunkenness, et cetera. If that happened with a soldier, then the military police would arrest that soldier. I don't know about the other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to move on and talk about the -- or ask you some questions about the work detail that you discuss in your statement, and that's at paragraph 15. You describe a -- you said the -- because of the difficulty at the front and the small number of men in Ozrenska Street you contacted the brigade, and a group of Muslim prisoners from Kula came and assisted in a work detail to reinforce a line. Now, how many days or weeks did this work detail spend at your Ozrenska Street positions fortifying the line ?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Since that was a period - it was still 1992 - we were unable to do this in any good way, we asked for help and perhaps seven or eight of them came. And again, I'm talking about the unit where I was in 1992. They were there for ten, maximum 12 days. I can't remember precisely anymore, but I know they were with us in our midst. They helped us and we fortified that line at Sanac together, the red line I drew on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what exactly did they do in terms of fortifying the line? Were they digging trenches? Building bunkers? What was their task?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Since that was in the immediate vicinity of the Pero Kosoric Square and the high-rises from which they were able to control the area, coming to that area was not safe for members of the VRS. So to just go there we had to make trenches and communicating trenches on arrival and we had to set up bunkers for the men whose job was to observe and to monitor and to scout and keep the line. Most of those communicating trenches which were perfectly visible from the high-rises, we had to put a cover over them. It's pointless to make communicating trenches if they can see you arriving. And one company commander was killed in that way when coming to inspect the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, we need to take a break now. We'll break for 40 minutes and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.51 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I point to one thing on the record, an imprecision on page 51, line 25. The witness said he had never been a member of the SDS but he knows that it - the record says "he" - it was a leader. That cannot be understood from the current LiveNote. In other words, it does not refer to a person, it refers to the SDS. And in our language "SDS" would be of the male gender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you refer to SDS when he was leader of the movement and concerned about the survival of Serb people, you meant the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. The SDS had the force of a movement in the Serbian movement. It does not refer to anyone individually, but the SDS as a political party which had the force of a movement for the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, just before the break I was asking you questions about the work detail of prisoners from Kula, and I understood from your last answer that this work detail was working on building bunkers and trenches and covering those trenches. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, digging communicating trenches as access to the trenches themselves where there was soldiers whose job it was to observe. In view of the vicinity of the positions from which fire was opened, these communicating trenches had to be covered from the top so that troops would be safe coming to and leaving the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said in your statement that you knew nothing else about these persons, other than that they were in prison at Kula. And it's also clear from your statement that you knew they were Muslim. Did you understand them to be civilians or prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I have no precise information that would enable me to give you a precise answer. I know that we approached the higher command, the brigade command, and to the extent they were able to, they sent us people for perhaps around 15 days until the line was completely fortified and we didn't need it anymore. I'm talking only about the unit where I was. There was no more need to engage anyone from the side. I don't know if they were prisoners, as you say, or civilians or -- I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now you've said that this work was being carried out in the immediate vicinity of Pero Kosoric Square, from which you've explained you faced incoming fire and were in constant danger, that this was between 20 and 50 metres away from the other side, and you've also said that this work was being carried out specifically because the VRS in that location was in danger. So I assume from all of that information that the Muslim prisoners engaged in this work detail were exposed to great danger of death or injury in carrying out this work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: That's not right. As soon as they arrived on the site, they started digging, and as soon as they would reach a certain depth we would cover that part. We did not subject them to great danger or danger of death by putting them there as sitting ducks. We were concerned about their security and we wanted them to fortify the line as soon as possible for our security and their own. When you come to a certain locality, you dig deep into the ground, and the earth that was dug out and the trench you dug out are immediately covered from view so that it would not be visible from Pero Kosoric Square or any other positions from which they could open fire on us and on the men working. So we did take care about their safety. Of course we told them not to try anything. We gave them the same food we had, we gave them cigarettes. And in that location, in the unit where I was, I was assistant platoon commander as I said before and the red line you showed on the map was the area of responsibility of that platoon, a length of about 300, 400 metres. There were really no incidents there. And from what I heard from some of those people who came there wanted to go out of wherever they were, to be in open air, they had better food, they got cigarettes from us, and we sometimes engaged in informal conversation about everyday things. But we never put them in any kind of danger. They were told that they were there to do their job. Nobody abused them in my unit, nobody mistreated them, and we were concerned about their safety as much as our own because our objective was to fortify the line as soon as possible to avoid further losses and we had already suffered losses in coming and going from the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now you've just said in that location where you were assistant platoon commander, there were really no incidents there; whereas earlier in your testimony when I asked you if you were in constant danger, you said something like particularly so. You agreed with that proposition wholeheartedly. Now in addition you've just said that as soon as these prisoners arrived on the site they started digging and "as soon as they would reach a certain depth we would cover that part." Now, even assuming that these prisoners would be protected once the trench was covered - I would think that would be a -- not a particularly safe assumption - before that trench is covered, when they have started digging, these prisoners were exposed to fire from the front line which was, as you said, 20 to 50 metres away, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Not from the moment of arrival to the line. The line of separation was 20 to 50 metres, but in order to reach those trenches the layout of the terrain would show that very clearly. It's an elevation and as soon as you reach the top, you are potentially a target of enemy fire. To avoid that -- we were actually with them while they were working. They could not do those works alone on any part of the line. There were always our own troops to take care of their safety and to prevent any untoward action on their part. They were told to behave when they arrived. And when I said there were no incidents, there were no incidents with the labour platoon. Nobody physically abused them, mistreated them, beat them, or threatened them, but they were told in advance just to do their job and everything would be all right, and that's how it was. The layout of the ground is such that it's an elevation, and when you come to the forward line you have to go there. It was as dangerous for them as it was for us. The Serb soldiers from the labour platoon were not any safer and that's the reason why we asked for someone to be sent, why they fortified the lines, and from that moment on, it was not necessary to engage them any longer. And they no longer came to my unit where I was assistant platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay if we could have 65 ter 1D02771, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, this is a report from the command of the 2nd Battalion, your battalion, to the administration of the Kula prison. And it says that: "Around 12.30 in the morning on the 21st of May, 1993, two Muslim prisoners who had been building bunkers with another nine prisoners escaped to the enemy side from the positions of our 4th Infantry Company in Ozrenska Street." And if you skip to the third paragraph, it says: "While they were working, Mitrovic guarded them with another two soldiers who were at the position there in a trench about 10 metres away from the prisoners. According to Mitrovic, the place where the work was carried out was constantly under infantry and rifle grenade fire from the enemy, and observation was difficult because it was dusk." If we can go to the next page in the English. It says: "Mitrovic found out about the escape when one of the prisoners ran to his trench and said to him, 'Zeka and Trifun have run away.' Mitrovic and the two soldiers who were with him immediately opened fire after the prisoners, but they did not prevent the escape." And then in the last paragraph it says: "We add that the work was carried out at night because that place was under constant enemy fire so it was impossible to carry out the work during the day. In addition, it is in the immediate vicinity of enemy positions." Now, this is a 4th Company report so it's from a position on Ozrenska Street down the street from where you were positioned, but this report explaining that the work of a detail of Muslim prisoners from Kula was being carried out under constant infantry and rifle grenade fire to the point that they were working at night because of the intensity of the fire. This report basically describes the conditions that Muslim prisoners from Kula faced in work details on Ozrenska Street; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: It says the 4th Infantry Company. That's not my area of responsibility. It's about 1500 metres from me, from my line. Doesn't this detail, that they were working by night, tell you that somebody was worried about their safety. It was too dangerous by the day, and I quite understand the commander or the assistant company commander to want to fortify that line because people were killed. So it was done by night. People were even buried by night at that time. You hear about those two, they escaped. I was not there but I heard about this incident, this escape. But somebody was obviously worried about their safety so they brought them to work there by night because it was too dangerous by day. But again, it was not in the area of my unit. I only know from other people about this escape by people from the labour platoon and I see the signature is the assistant commander for security, lieutenant or lieutenant second class Dragan Maletic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the third line there is a passive form: People were buried. Whereas the witness said: We buried our casualties by night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, the use of these Muslim prisoners to carry out work such as building bunkers and digging trenches on the front line at Ozrenska Street, not only did it violate basic provisions of the Geneva Conventions requiring the humane treatment of prisoners of war and civilians; it also violates the prohibition in the Geneva Conventions of using either prisoners of war or civilians in work that is directly related to military activities, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is misleading. [In English] This is misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what basis? I assume --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that roads were accessible, not the forward line, and he never said they were digging the forward lines and trenches there. They were digging only for road works.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's absolutely false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think -- please continue. You can take up that issue in your re-examination, but I don't think Ms. Gustafson was misleading. He can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. This use of Muslim prisoners to carry out work such as building bunkers and digging trenches on the front line at Ozrenska Street, not only did it violate basic provisions of the Geneva Conventions requiring the humane treatment of prisoners of war and civilians, it also violates the prohibition in the conventions of using either prisoners of war or civilians in work that is directly related to military activities, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Our motivation and our desire was primarily to protect personnel. Throughout the war, we had problems filling our ranks due to a great number of casualties and woundings. We did not have enough people, and that's why we asked for assistance from a higher command to send people in a way that would provide a solution once and for all. They were digging access to the line, and of course with the bunkers that we were fortifying, they were helping it all. But we used them as we needed to, to be able to observe a position and open fire from those bunkers if we were attacked. So they did not give us conceptual solutions as to how to do that. They helped us only in one part. Their work was completely safe. We were as concerned about their safety as we were about ours. They received the same food as we did, and as soon as they were done they would leave. That's how it was arranged in my unit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be shown where in the document is it stated that they were digging trenches on the forward line, on the first line?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, this -- the question wasn't about this specific document, but the document says that these prisoners were building bunkers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5987, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, I'd like to move on to another part of your statement where you said at paragraph 23 that UN military observers would come to the battalion command, so this is at a time when you were in the battalion command, to investigate firing incidents, and you said you would take them to the alleged fire positions where they would be assured that the Serbian side did not commit the alleged fire and they never had complaints about your unit. Now if we could go to Exhibit D2421 which is a document you discuss in your statement at paragraph 26. And this is an order to -- from the battalion command to the 4th Company which states that foreign military observers have received permission to monitor the cease-fire in the battalion's zone of responsibility. In the second paragraph it explains when the monitoring will commence and the licence plate numbers of the vehicles that will be used. And the substance of the order is in the final paragraph where it says: "Facilitate the movement of the military observers in your zone of responsibility, but prevent their direct access to our positions and their surveillance of the same without permission. If they should request it, seek the approval of the battalion command. If they are found at positions without approval, detain them and report to the battalion command." Now, the standing order in this document is to prevent the access and surveillance of the unit's position and sets out the steps to be followed if such access is requested. Is that a fair reading?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Just one correction. You said a moment ago that I was battalion commander. At this time, look at the signature, this is deputy battalion commander Mr. Hrvatcevic, while Mr. Petrovic was commander. I was assistant battalion commander. It says enable military observers to move. It even lists vehicles to be given to them, to make everything possible for them. But if they come directly into the trench, we cannot be absolutely sure, although they are coming as an unbiased impartial organisation, we could never be sure whether they could pass on the information to the other side. Why am I saying this? Because this was the B team of military observers, whereas the A team was in the city in the PTT engineering building, and a Jordanian man was the boss of both. He co-ordinated both A and B teams. A was on the Muslim side; B was on the Serb side. The order was clear: Enable their movement. But please, to allow them to come into every trench to see how many people we have, how many weapons we have, I don't know who would have allowed that. They were told they can come anywhere they like. And on the Muslim side, there were always violations of the cease-fire. They repaired their fortifications, et cetera. And when we asked them - we from the battalion command - based on reports from lower units, when we asked them to check on those incidents and violations, they would have to call the A team, and this happened a thousand times, the Muslims would stop their works. And in their eyes, there was always this impression that we were making things up, until one time when they actually realised it was true. Their crew went out and found the Muslims doing that. But it was necessary to get the green light from the Jordanian man for either crew to go out on the site and verify our claims or theirs. Of course, they were allowed to move, but there are certain limits and rules of conduct. I don't see from this order, although I know about the commander and the deputy commander, perhaps this was a -- I came to the command in the beginning of June --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: -- this is 26th of May, but I know about this --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- I think again we're straying a little far from the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P1822. This is a UN military observer report. If we could go to page 2 of the report, this is from the 11th of August, 1994, and it describes a follow-up investigation after the shooting of an 11-year-old girl in Sarajevo by a 12.7-millimetre weapon. And it says: "UNMO patrols were sent out on both sides of the confrontation line in the Grbavica area." And in paragraph 2 it states that: "The team was able to bearing on a point which coincided with a new 12.7-millimetre position that was known to the team." And in paragraph 3 it says: "The UNMO patrol was sent to the location but was delayed by Bosnian Serb army forces who insisted that the patrol get clearance ... clearance that they had already received." And then it says: "Finally after some time going back and forth ... the patrol was allowed to the site. By this time the 12.7-millimetre gun had been removed. The soldiers at the position stated it had been taken away for maintenance." Now, this is clearly in the area of the 2nd Battalion and this document - noting the superfluous clearance demands and the delays that were sufficient that the suspected weapon in question had been removed - this reflects an effort by forces within your battalion to obstruct the effective monitoring of the cease-fire; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct and I'll explain why. I was right there. I think the incident involves two little girls, if that's the same incident. There were two girls there. When I was in the battalion command we received a report from the company command that two little girls, perhaps around 10, were hit. And then I informed the B team of military observers by courier - the man number one in that team was a Swedish captain - and they went out. I can only understand this as an expression of anger of troops who happened to be there. But I was personally there with the Swedish captain. We went down there. We took the girls to the Kasindol hospital and we were all horrified over that. It looked as if somebody took the scalp off these girls. It's a destructive calibre --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, I think you're misunderstanding. I think you're confusing this -- the incident described here with an incident you describe in your statement about the killing of two Serb girls from the Muslim side, and incident with the Chamber has received evidence occurred on the 11th of March, 1995, and I'd refer to D2294 and P879 as references. This is an incident that's describing the alleged striking of a young girl from the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation line into the -- so the victim in question was on the Muslim side of the line.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: In Grbavica? It says here that the incident happened in Grbavica, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't think that's right. It gives a grid reference in Sarajevo, but the -- and the investigation took place in Grbavica. So I understand -- if that's the case, do you not have a recollection of this incident?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with this. You're right, I obviously had in mind another incident. I'm not familiar with this case. What happened, sniper, 12.7 -- I don't even know that such a weapon existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So then you can't comment on the extent to which the Bosnian Serb army obstructed --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No, really --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- sorry, you can't comment on --

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. I'm not familiar with this case. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd just like that ask you a more general question. You've said -- you've emphasized in your statement and in your evidence today your view that the Bosnian Serb side scrupulously complied with the laws of war. Did you ever hear anything from any source that the SRK was targeting civilians in Sarajevo, particularly through shelling and sniping? Did information to that effect ever come to your attention at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies. I have to shed light on some of the things that appeared during cross-examination. Can we look at D426. D426.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier today you were shown one part of a document --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D426, D426.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Earlier today you were shown a part of a document in which Mr. Prstojevic addressed the president. Let's look at bullet point 3 to see what my position was with regard to the civilian population. Could you please read bullet point 3 aloud. Please read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: You want me to read it out? Under 3 it says: "To spare the civilians of all attacks."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to call up D92. This was also shown to you before. Could we get page 87 in Serbian and 86 in English. This was not shown to you. This is an excerpt from an Assembly session. Could you please look at line 9 from the top in the Serbian version of the document. Line 9 from the bottom. Can we scroll up a little to display that line. It says here: "In that state which we are building, we have to provide them with all the rights that we ourselves have ..." How does this tally with your notions of our policies, of my policies, with regard to other ethnic communities and people? How does this correspond to what you know about my position with regard to other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I can't see anything here. Any democratic system in the world would be happy if something like that were said. It says here that we guarantee all rights to everybody unless they harbour hostile intentions. This is an encouragement to all those who want to live in Republika Srpska. This can only encourage them to stay in their homes and to continue living where they have always lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have just shown you bullet point 3 which was issued before this Assembly session. This is the Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now look at D7154 -- D1754. D1754, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at bullet point 3, it's not very legible. I'm going to try and read it. There has to be an English translation because this document has been admitted into evidence already. Bullet point 3, I'm going to read that: "Forced transfer of people and other illegal measures against civilian population must be prevented; certificates on property selling or written statements by refugees that they will not return, if any, are not legally valid and are out of force." I believe that this was issued in August, on the 17th of August. How does this fit with your understanding of our policies?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: This is the only correct understanding. There is no forced transfer. I claimed in my statement that no such things ever happened. Are you talking about the document that was issued on the 13th of June, 1992? That's a document that I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "According to our official act of June 13 ..." That was the first such document and this one was issued on the 19th of August. If we scroll up we will see it.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: The way I perceive it is as an encouragement and a guarantee to those who decide to stay, who have never harboured any hostile activities, who are not involved in acts of terrorism. It says here that forced transfer should be banned, that property looting should be banned, and if anybody engaged in such activities they would be duly punished. That's how I perceive this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown something that concerned my speech in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up D1270.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were suggested outside of any context that I had delivered a speech which was war-mongering or intimidating. Let's look at page 116 in Serbian, or rather, in English and in Serbian it's 122. This was issued on the 14th of October when there was out-voting and when a declaration on sovereignty was passed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read the first paragraph. "Before any explanation of the proposal is proposed, I don't know whether I'm going to explain it or somebody else, I have to clarify one thing which arises from the interpretation of what is being said from this place. And this concerns the issue of war or peace. For the umpteenth time I have to repeat that Serbs are not threatening to wage a war. Serbs only declared that they would not be able to accept any decision which is issued by means of out-voting and to their detriment." And one more thing on this page, a little bit further down, somewhere in the middle of the page it says: "Serbs never attacked Muslims nor will they ever attack Muslims. There is no such a feeling towards Muslims; however, the case that could arise from decisions passed by out-voting, the case that could arise that will not be launched by anybody but it will follow its own logic of what we've spoken here. This is not chaos; order lies in our hands. Chaos is not in anybody's hands. The main characteristics of chaos is the fact that nobody generates it. It follows its own logic and it is self-generating."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page. It should be 117 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I just ask that Mr. Karadzic indicate where in this transcript it says that Serbs never attacked Muslims nor will they ever attack Muslims. I couldn't find that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- spilling over to page 117 in English. [In English] Serbs never attacked -- [Interpretation] Last line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on it says, talking about chaos -- can we move to the following page both in Serbian and in English. It says here: What else could the Serbs offer, although we wholeheartedly accept Mr. Izetbegovic's proposal. I can see that there are no positions [as interpreted] to that in the Croatian Democratic Union. Let's think about that. Let's talk to the world about Bosnia-Herzegovina, about Croats, Muslims, and Serbs. Let's convey a message that there won't be a war. Serbs will not be forced to accept one option and Muslims and Croats another one. We can send the message that there won't be a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We can guarantee that there won't be chaos because order is in our hands. Chaos is no longer in anybody's hands. On this occasion I convey warm messages and greetings to Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, to common people who don't even know what sovereignty is, who don't know what the change of a constitutional and legal position is, who are not aware of the projection of things that will be Bosnia in two or four or five years. My message to them is to support us in our intention for the war not to take place. I'm conveying warm messages, not war messages, but warm messages, warm. Once again let's convey warm messages and greetings to all the three peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let's tell them that we are taking all measures to avoid war, to avoid out-voting and so on and so forth. In your experience, would you call this war-mongering or would you call this a message against war?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: It would be a message anti-war. In my statement and during my examination I remember the Lisbon Agreement and we sincerely hoped that war would be avoided. I suppose that all the members of the other peoples hoped the same. I really didn't -- never understood why the Muslims had given up on that agreement which was a guarantee of security for everybody, which was a guarantee that war would not take place and everything could have ended up peacefully. War is terrible for everybody. I no longer live in my own city, a city where I have lived all my life. This is tragic and it is tragic for everybody who left their homes, especially those who lost somebody in that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier today you were shown some of the diary notes by General Mladic, page 53.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 7845.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your answer was that that did not concern Muslims but rather the Muslim police who might jeopardise safety and security. Please look at the document. This is an UNPROFOR report on a visit to Grbavica. It says on the 9th of March, 1993 -- [In English] Visit protection officer to Grbavica on March the 18th, 1993. [Interpretation] And then bullet point 4: Minorities. [In English] "There are approximately 1.200 Muslims still in Grbavica. The males are not drafted, but those of a certain age have to do work for -- between 100 and 150 Muslims have indicated a willingness to leave to the other side [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. Is it true that at that time there were about 1200 Muslims, that you did not mobilise them, but some had work obligation? And was it only Muslims who had work obligation or was it everybody?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any precise information. I know that there were a lot of Muslims and I've already said that today. I know that a lot of Muslims lived in Grbavica, especially in the part where there were expulsions. Many people lived there. I didn't know this information - it's UNPROFOR information. There was a work obligation for everyone who was not a member of military units. Although I had nothing to do with this personally, I know that some reported for work. When humanitarian aid convoys arrived, they would help with the unloading of the goods, they were still receiving them at the time. Since that was the situation in Sarajevo, there weren't enough goods, people were willing to work on humanitarian products in order to receive some humanitarian aid which they received as did all the other inhabitants. I didn't know that there were so many of them, but there certainly were a lot of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it says that they registered a hundred and 150 of them who wanted to cross over. Was this prevented when such wishes were expressed?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: No. This information is from 1993. As I said, at the time I was in my unit's sector. I know that there was a large group that crossed over, perhaps 200 people, but I have no idea. I know that they managed to cross over. One part of that group crossed over the Bratstvo i Jedinstvo Bridge and the other part crossed over a smaller bridge across the road from Hotel Bristol. That bridge linked the left bank and the right bank in the vicinity of Hotel Bristol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And later you were in the battalion. Did Muslims remain living there - I won't ask you about the number - throughout the war, as well as Croats? Did they remain in Grbavica, those who didn't want to leave?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many of them remained there, especially Muslims. I don't know how many Croats, though, I don't have any exact numbers, but I know for certain that they continued living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is this related to Mladic -- the part of the Mladic diary that we saw earlier on? Mladic diary was dated 1995, after the Dayton, and this is 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. But there it said that Mr. Tomic was against the return of Muslims, Muslim civilians, and in the other place it said the police and the authorities, not civilians. So this shows that civilians always lived there throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document shows that there were 1200 Muslims in 1993. In any event, I'll leave it at that. Let's continue. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2424.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D3709.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention to the fact this is an order to carry out combat operations in the Grbavica sector. It was signed by the commander of the 1st Motorised Brigade, the 1st Muslim Motorised Brigade. It was authorised by the commander of the 1st Corps, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, Talijan. The 2nd of January, 1993, is the date. Now I would like to remind you of your testimony according to which you weren't afraid of civilians returning, you were afraid of armed forces returning, armed forces, the police and the Muslim authorities. Could we now see the next page. In the English version too. Please, let's have a look at the part in a box that says: "Task." The 31st of December, it's just before the new year, New Year's Eve, and it says: "Task. Take the the sector to the right, Tranzit to the left, the bridge by Elektroprivreda, carry out an attack on the following axis: 11 Plavi, the southern part of the state in Grbavica, Palma, the Soping and Strojorad, four large skyscrapers, with the objective of routing the enemy on these axes and taking control of important features." Can we see the following page, please. And could we see the following page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We only have this part translated in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item number 6, paragraph number 6, fire support. The artillery shall provide fire support in the enemy's depth at the command post, post where the reserves are deployed, in accordance with the requests from the battalion commander. Can we see the following page, it's the same page in the English version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, before you continue with this question, can you explain what this document is about and then can you also explain why the format of the document looks like this? It seems like you cut and pasted this document from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this is an IDS document. It's a Muslim order for an offensive on Grbavica. We only have this part translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the most salient part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't explain -- answer my question, my question why the fonts per paragraph look -- differs. Para 3, para 4, and para 6, they all look different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, it's -- it was typed on a Muslim machine. They added things to it. It took a while to compile the order. It wasn't all done in one go, but the original is theirs. It's signed on the first page so it's their document. The question is when they added certain elements and to which parts of the order. You also have a stamp at the end of the document, at the bottom of the document, and it also bears a signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I also see the ERN number. Is it from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It certainly appears to be the case from the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at the next page, please, in the Serbian version, the same page in the English version. Could we have a look at the last paragraph just above "logistics support," could we scroll up a bit. I'll read it out. "Since taking such a fortified settlement is impossible without destroying and torching features which are strong fortifications at the same time everything has to be destroyed and torched. To carry out the operation in -- safely because of the brazenness, the lack of principles, one shouldn't trust a single captive and especially not captives bearing weapons of any kind." I'm waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, is such an approach of the ABiH towards captives, settlements, and features, did such an approach have an influence on you and on the inhabitants of Grbavica when it came to waiting for the Muslim police and authorities after the Dayton --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure a sufficient foundation for that question has been asked. I mean, it is -- the question assumes -- first of all, this witness's knowledge of this specific attack; secondly, that it was effectively carried out. I mean, we know nothing about that at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to respond to Ms. Gustafson's observation or would you like to reformulate your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During this period of time were you in Grbavica, the 2nd of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war-time period, as I have already said, until I went to the battalion command I was in a unit sector above the Tranzit and the stadium in Sansa [phoen] sector. I was in the command battalion from June 1994. I never saw this document, but there were a lot of Serbs who fled at lines in our area of responsibility. And we obtained a lot of information from them about this. So it wasn't even necessary for me to see such a document. Naturally I was concerned about my safety and the safety of my family and of my friends. So I don't know who had a diary. We didn't sign things. I didn't sign things like my statement -- well, I stand behind everything I said at Mr. Mladic's meeting. I didn't receive the minutes, I didn't sign anything. I didn't say the Muslims could not return, but in January 1996 if we remain there, if their police or military arrived -- well, what would have happened? No one would have been safe and especially not those who were members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there such attacks and how many such attacks were there on Grbavica and on your area, Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say, I couldn't give you a precise number, but there were many attacks on all the lines. Sometimes this was simulated, but most of the attacks would be carried out against some other line, but we kept increasing the level of combat-readiness, we were often at full combat-readiness, so people were very tired, exhausted, because there were constant attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was there such destruction of buildings, such torching of buildings and features?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Where you have this -- these special types of ammunition, whenever possible they would torch things. When I was visiting a command line I entered the nearest -- the building that was nearest to the Strojorad, the skyscraper nearest to it. This was at the end of 1994. A soldier of ours who was living there and remained there, his family had been settled in the inner part of Grbavica, he told me that only that skyscraper was on fire 44 times. This is close to the Miljacka river, to Strojorad. That is where a line of disengagement was, in fact. It was about 30 or 50 metres from the bank of the Miljacka. So they used these flares, as I said, this type of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you understand this advice, don't trust a single POW?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know how the interpreter will translate this, interpret this. I'm trying to be as precise as possible. The proverb is: Gestures are sufficient for a clever person. How can I draw any other conclusion from this? It concerns people who have weapons with them. I don't know where -- what the rules are, but that is how I interpreted this. It means: Eliminate everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think in Latin one says "sapienti sat," what you just said. Thank you. Can we see the last page, the signature. To be frank, Zlatko Lagumdzija isn't the politician, is he? This is a commander. It says: Commander Zlatko Lagumdzija. It's not the politician Zlatko Lagumdzija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want us to be frank. It wouldn't be fair if we suggested in public that this was the name of the politician because there is a well-known politician whose name is Zlatko Lagumdzija. Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness was really able to confirm that anything like what is described in this document took place and it would certainly be news to the Court that there was, in fact, a major offensive in Grbavica at the date that this document states.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the witness has indicated that this is consistent with his observations and concerns about police coming into Serb areas, and I think that on that basis - since he's indicated it's consistent with his understanding - that it's admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it that the Prosecution is not challenging the authenticity about this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we -- we have to look into it. I agree with Your Honour's observations that it's an odd-looking document, but I simply can't comment at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The special type of ammunition the witness referred to earlier was, in fact, armour-piercing incendiary bullets, not flares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of relevance, the Chamber tends to agree with Mr. Robinson, but given the authenticity issue as well as the English translation, simply it is lacking. So we mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to call up 1D500.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my last question about your concern and the concern of Serbs in Grbavica with regard to those who may be allowed to return. Unfortunately, this is yet another untranslated document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that on-site translations in the courtroom cannot be taken as official translations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This bulletin of the staff of the Supreme Command of armed forces which was issued on the 11th of October, 1993. Can we please look at page 3 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the part of the document which is in a frame.

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: "Among the combatants of the 101st Motorised Brigade who are mostly not satisfied with the work of the command of this unit, there has been a rumour going on recently that the command in the locality in the zone of responsibility of this battalion should be taken over by Musan Topalovic - Caco. The commander of the 1st [as interpreted] Motorised Battalion, Enis Srna, who, according to some unverified sources, is in cahoots with Caco, commented upon this rumour with the following words: 'In tactical terms it is better for one person to be in charge of Grbavica so that it could be cleansed.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the people who are mentioned in here?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I did hear about Musan Topalovic, Caco. I did not hear about Enis Srna. That name doesn't ring bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who they cleanse Grbavica from [as interpreted], what does this imply?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: I believe that it is more than clear. This is a threat addressed at the Serbian population, at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber who was Musan Topalovic, Caco, what was his reputation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes -- no, just a second, Mr. Tomic. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This doesn't seem to relate to the cross-examination. I'm not sure what the connection is supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question is whether there was any reason for the Serbs in Grbavica to be afraid of Musan Topalovic, Caco -- [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This arises from contesting that the Serbian population in Grbavica was afraid of the arrival of the Muslim police and the army, i.e., the authorities. Now I'm asking the witness whether he knows Musan Topalovic, Caco, and whether his reputation gave enough reason for fear among the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Whether or not the Serbian population in Grbavica was afraid or not was not an issue that was raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer or should I repeat?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat. I never met Musan Topalovic, Caco, personally, but everybody in Sarajevo was aware of his reputation and, of course, our fear was justified. We were afraid if something like that should happen, we knew what would have happened to us, especially us who were members of the Army of Republika Srpska. So the fear was justified, it was present and justified.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I -- since Your Honour's allowed the question I won't object to the marking of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2426.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Can I have a five-minute break to go to the bathroom if at all possible. I need three minutes -- a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have further questions, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three or four short questions, but I think that the witness should be allowed to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. --- Break taken at 2.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, I thought that was the last question from you, but please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let it then be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you were asked about M84 and M53 Brownings and so on and so forth and about their ranges. When it comes to these weapons, were they used in the Ozrenska zone of the entire battalion, could they be used for sniper fire and killing civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOZO TOMIC
utterances.text: Those weapons were used only in support in case of attack, to allow us to defend ourselves, because M84 is a good weapon, a well-tested weapon. In my statement I already stated that M53 is not a reliable machine-gun. From those weapons you couldn't open sniper fire. They don't have optical sights. For example, M53 doesn't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for coming to testify. I have no further questions. I would have a lot more questions but they're not that pertinent, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness has answered the question already, but please refrain from asking leading questions, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to add that that was -- the issue of sniping was never raised either in direct or in cross-examination and it's totally unfair to put that as the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the subject was raised, Mr. Witness, but if the line of separation was only 50 to 80 yards, you wouldn't need optical sights, would you, because a competent rifle shooter over 50 or 80 metres would be able to shoot with his eye on the sights without an optical enhancement. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be heard? May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No, this is to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond to Madam Gustafson's objection? This is what I would like to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure you followed. Judge Morrison was asking a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But -- but, no, no, not to Judge Morrison, no, not to Judge Morrison. I would like to respond to Madam Gustafson. In cross-examination Madam Gustafson laid a foundation for the incident that happened in Krndelja Street and so on and so forth. Those were sniping incidents. I wanted to establish what that was about because that was about precision and range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's moot already now, so I'll leave it at that. So, Mr. Tomic, do you remember Judge Morrison's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember the question properly, His Excellency Judge Morrison stated, as a matter of fact, that at such short distances you don't need optical sights and I fully agree with that. However, I was answering Mr. Karadzic's questions and I said that one could not open in -- fire a single shot from those weapons. You could only fire bursts of fire, and those weapons were not used to open fire in depth. They were only used in cases of attack and in cases when you wanted to repel an attack. M53 and M84 weapons were not used because they opened bursts of fire and they're not as precise as the types of weapons which fire single shots. Although His Excellency, Judge Morrison, is absolutely right. At such short distances we did not use optical sights because they were not needed. There is a good line of visibility at distances of 50 to 80 yards as Mr. Morrison said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that seems to conclude your evidence, Mr. Tomic. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, and on my behalf I would like to commend the services that have looked after my arrival and stay here in The Hague and everything else. Once again, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll rise all together. I was informed by the Registry that the -- due to technical difficulties, Courtroom 1 will be closed down for renovation in terms of a switchboard. So tomorrow we'll be sitting in the afternoon in Courtroom 3 after Mladic trial, i.e., from 2.15 to 7.00. On Thursday, we'll sit in the morning from 9.00 to quarter to 2.00 in Courtroom 3. So I appreciate the Registry's endeavour to get the proceedings to go on. Given the time and given that the Chamber needs to rise at 3.00 sharp, so we'll adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of November, 2012, at 2.15 p.m.
